findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Make the portable tests independent of real ssh-keygen permission checks: fake `ssh-keygen` too (or assert ordering via a spy on `_write_copy`), and state how the success-path tests behave on Windows and POSIX.
evidence: "Portable (all platforms; `_POSIX_MODE_BITS` forced False; ... passes `ssh-keygen` to the real `run`)"
Context: the copy takes mkdtemp's DACL (SYSTEM, Administrators, OWNER RIGHTS), which ssh-keygen rejects
findings.finding: The portable tests fake `whoami`/`icacls` but pass `ssh-keygen` to the real `run`, and they are declared to run on all platforms. On a Windows runner the fake icacls changes nothing, so the copy keeps the mkdtemp OWNER RIGHTS ACE. The real `ssh-keygen -y` will then reject it with 'Bad permissions' and `compose_signer` will raise. The ordering, timeout, SID-skip and non-ASCII tests will therefore fail, or pass only by accident, on Windows. On POSIX, forcing `_POSIX_MODE_BITS` False may also change how the copy is written, and real ssh-keygen may then reject a non-0600 file.
scenarios: The Windows sweep runs `test_opcert_key_copy_windows_acl.py`; the portable success-path tests raise OpcertKeyError from ssh-keygen.
On Linux with the mode switch forced False, the copy is written without a 0600 chmod and ssh-keygen reports UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE.
findings.suggested_fix: In the portable tests, have the fake also answer `ssh-keygen` with a canned success (public-key output). Assert the ordering by recording `whoami`, `icacls`, `icacls` and then a `_write_copy` spy. Leave real ssh-keygen only to the Windows-guarded test.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the rebar-mcp ordering claim: the store-sweep daemon always starts before `compose_signer`; the idle-sync daemon starts first only on the HTTP transport (mcp_server.py:583-591).
evidence: Plan: "in `rebar-mcp` it runs after the store-sweep and idle-sync daemon threads start, and the error leaves `main()` and ends the process"

src/rebar/mcp_server.py:583-591: `start_startup_store_sweep(...)` always; `if cfg.mcp.transport == "http": start_idle_sync(...)`; then `binding = compose_startup_opcert_binding(cfg)` outside the try/finally
src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:404,492: both are started on daemon threads via `spawn_context_daemon`
findings.finding: The Failure-disposition bullet says that in `rebar-mcp`, `compose_signer` runs after the store-sweep and idle-sync daemon threads start. In the code, only the store-sweep starts every time; idle-sync starts only when `cfg.mcp.transport == "http"`. On the stdio transport, no idle-sync thread is running when the new error is raised.
findings.location: Approach — Failure disposition bullet (rebar-mcp startup ordering)
scenarios: A stdio rebar-mcp session on Windows whose `icacls` call fails: only the boot store-sweep thread exists when `OpcertKeyError` leaves `main()`.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword to: "in `rebar-mcp` it runs after the boot store-sweep daemon thread starts (and, on the HTTP transport, the idle-sync daemon thread); both are daemon threads, so the error leaves `main()` and ends the process."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In Testing, state that `_write_copy` creates the copy owner-only (0600) regardless of `_POSIX_MODE_BITS`, or have the fake also answer `ssh-keygen` in the portable order/timeout tests so they do not depend on POSIX key-permission checks.
evidence: '`_POSIX_MODE_BITS` forced False; ... a fake that answers `whoami`/`icacls` by `argv[0]` and passes `ssh-keygen` to the real `run`'
The plan does not say whether `_write_copy`'s file mode depends on `_POSIX_MODE_BITS`.
findings.finding: The portable tests run the real `ssh-keygen` on POSIX hosts with `_POSIX_MODE_BITS` forced False. They therefore rely on an unstated assumption: that the copy `compose_signer` writes is still owner-only (0600) under the forced switch. POSIX ssh-keygen refuses a private key file with group/other read bits ('UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE'). If the switch also changes how `_write_copy` sets the copy's mode, the portable tests fail on Linux/macOS for a reason unrelated to the DACL logic.
findings.location: Testing — 'Portable (all platforms; `_POSIX_MODE_BITS` forced False; ... passes `ssh-keygen` to the real `run`)'
scenarios: On a Linux CI host, the forced-False switch skips a chmod/0600 step in the copy path. The real `ssh-keygen -y` then rejects the copy with a permissions error, and the order/timeout tests fail spuriously.

Retrieved: github.com/python/cpython/issues/118486, "[CVE-2024-4030] Enable `mkdir(mode=0o700)` to work on Windows"; follow-up "gh-118486: Switch mkdir(mode=0o700) on Windows to use OWNER RIGHTS instead of CURRENT_USER #118515"
Retrieved: python.org Python 3.9.20 release notes: "gh-118486: os.mkdir() on Windows now accepts mode of 0o700 ... fixes CVE-2024-4030 affecting tempfile.mkdtemp()" (so not specific to 3.13)
Retrieved: github.com/PowerShell/Win32-OpenSSH/issues/2317, "OWNER RIGHTS not allowed on identity file ACL, even if owner is in..." ("OpenSSH fails Bad permissions")
pyproject.toml: requires-python = ">=3.11"
findings.finding: The plan's root-cause record does not cite the upstream sources that already describe this interaction: CPython gh-118486 / CVE-2024-4030 (os.mkdir(mode=0o700) on Windows, used by tempfile.mkdtemp, writes an OWNER RIGHTS-based protected DACL; backported to security releases, not 3.13-only) and PowerShell/Win32-OpenSSH issue #2317 (OWNER RIGHTS not allowed on an identity-file ACL). Without them the ticket presents a known upstream incompatibility as a local finding. It also records no exit condition for removing the workaround if Win32-OpenSSH starts accepting OWNER RIGHTS.
findings.location: Context / Problem; Hypotheses ("the ACE comes from `tempfile.mkdtemp`'s DACL")
scenarios: A maintainer later sees Win32-OpenSSH #2317 fixed upstream and cannot tell from the ticket whether the icacls step can be removed
Someone reading 'Python 3.13's mkdtemp' assumes 3.11/3.12 hosts are unaffected, although the CVE fix was backported to security releases
findings.suggested_fix: In Context / Problem, replace "the DACL Python 3.13's `tempfile.mkdtemp` writes" with "the protected OWNER RIGHTS DACL that `os.mkdir(mode=0o700)` writes on Windows since CPython gh-118486 / CVE-2024-4030 (used by `tempfile.mkdtemp`; backported to security releases)". Add: "Win32-OpenSSH rejects OWNER RIGHTS on key files (PowerShell/Win32-OpenSSH#2317); the module comment on `_restrict_dir_to_owner` names that issue."

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] In the Mechanism choice bullet, name the SDDL-string in-process route (as in CPython's gh-118486 os.mkdir implementation) and say why icacls/whoami subprocesses are still preferred, instead of rejecting ctypes only for 'hand-written structure'.
evidence: Plan: "Rejected: building the DACL in-process via the Win32 API over `ctypes`, which needs hand-written structure and handle management with no repo precedent."
Retrieved: github.com/python/cpython/issues/118486, where CPython applies the 0o700 DACL in-process on Windows (switched to OWNER RIGHTS in #118515)

The plan adds three subprocess calls, a 60s timeout constant, CSV parsing and four failure modes (missing tool, timeout, non-zero exit, unparseable output), all of which the rejection reason is meant to justify
findings.finding: The plan rejects the in-process route because it 'needs hand-written structure and handle management'. The obvious prior art, CPython's own os.mkdir(0o700) Windows implementation from gh-118486, does the in-process work from a security-descriptor string rather than hand-built ACL structures. The plan does not weigh that SDDL route. So the stated reason for choosing two subprocess tools plus CSV parsing (with the timeouts and failure modes that brings) over an in-process call is partly wrong.
scenarios: A reviewer comparing options takes the ctypes route to be much heavier than it is and never checks the SDDL path

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the default: every restriction failure, including whoami/SID-read failures, raises OpcertKeyError whose message starts with `cannot restrict the op-cert key copy`; assert that prefix in each portable failure test.
evidence: "raises `OpcertKeyError` with a message beginning `cannot restrict the op-cert key copy` (or naming the SID read) so it is distinguishable"
Testing: "... raises `OpcertKeyError` and leaves no `rebar-opcert-*` dir behind" (no message assertion)
findings.finding: The error-message contract is ambiguous: 'a message beginning `cannot restrict the op-cert key copy` (or naming the SID read)'. It does not say what the whoami-failure message starts with. The tests only assert that `OpcertKeyError` is raised, so nothing checks that these failures are 'distinguishable from the existing key-content rejections'.
findings.location: Approach, 'Failure disposition' bullet; Testing, Portable bullet
scenarios: An implementer wraps the error in the existing 'malformed, encrypted ... unusable' message, and every test still passes.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the single prefix `cannot restrict the op-cert key copy:` followed by the failing step (e.g. `reading the current user's SID`, `icacls grant`, `icacls remove`). In each failure-case test, add `assert str(exc).startswith('cannot restrict the op-cert key copy')`.
